belief: “I can’t manage life without someone to lean on.”
belief_plain: I can’t manage life without someone to lean on.
intro: Do you feel lost or panicky when you are on your own, as if you could not manage without a particular person? The information below is intended to help you take a step toward quiet confidence, and to find the strength that comes from knowing God’s word as found in the Bible.
origins: Some people never had the chance to learn they could cope. A parent who did everything, or a parent who was unreliable and left them anxious, can leave a person doubting their own ability. Later, one person comes to feel like the only source of steadiness, so the thought of losing them feels like losing the ability to live.
keeps: Leaning heavily on one person leaves less practice at handling things alone, and less practice feeds the doubt. I may also stay in unhealthy situations or avoid disagreement to keep the person close. Each time I get through a hard moment, I may credit the other person instead of myself.
teaches: God made us for one another, and leaning on others is healthy: “Two are better than one.” But our deepest support is God Himself: “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.” Even when we feel weak, “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.” We can say with Paul, “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.” The goal is not to lean on no one, but to rest on God first and to share life with others freely.
key: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.
also: Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My right hand of righteousness.
I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.
My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.
Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor. For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!
self: I cannot do this on my own.
I would fall apart without them.
I do not know how to handle things.
I cannot be left on my own.
errors: Imagining that being alone would be unbearable.
Predicting that I would not cope.
Believing I am either supported or helpless.
Overlooking the times I have handled things myself.
Feeling panicky and concluding I cannot cope.
Calling myself helpless instead of describing a struggle.
questions: What have I handled on my own before?
What exactly do I think would happen if this person were away?
Is it true I have no skills, or have I just had little practice?
How has God helped me in past hard times?
What is one small thing I could do for myself this week?
Is it healthy to lean on others while also standing on my own?
What would I tell a friend who felt this way?
truth: I can share life with others, and I can also stand. God is my refuge and strength, and I have handled hard things before. Being alone for a time does not mean being helpless. I can grow in confidence one small step at a time.
prayer: Lord, You are my refuge and strength. Help me to rest in You first, to grow in confidence, and to share life with others without losing myself. Amen.
clinical: For counselors: this belief appears in the cognitive model of what clinicians call borderline personality disorder (Beck, Davis, & Freeman, Cognitive Therapy of Personality Disorders), where fear of abandonment, all-or-nothing thinking about people, an unsettled sense of self, and a fear of being overwhelmed by emotion are central. Dependence on a single attachment figure and fear of being unable to cope alone are common; build self-efficacy through graded independence tasks, and distinguish healthy interdependence from avoidance of one’s own competence. Behavioral skills for tolerating distress and regulating emotion (as in Linehan’s DBT) pair well with this card’s Identify → Challenge → Replace work. Screen for self-harm and suicide risk, and consult or refer when risk is present (in the U.S., 988). This is an individualized educational formulation, not a DSM criterion or a diagnostic test. Similar presentations can arise from trauma, depression, anxiety, or temperament, so careful assessment matters. Pace any experiments to the person.
morning: Each morning ask: “What is one thing I can do on my own today, with God’s help?”
hw_truths: God is my refuge and strength.
I have handled hard things before.
I can stand and still share life.
I can grow in confidence one step at a time.
experiments: List three hard things you have handled before.
Do one small task on your own that you usually ask someone to help with.
Spend an hour alone and note how you coped.
Make one small decision without asking for reassurance.
Pray Psalm 46:1 when you feel helpless.
Thank someone who supports you, and tell them one thing you did yourself.
reflect: After listening to one of the four songs, write a sentence about God’s strength.
newtruth: God is my strength. I have handled hard things, and I can stand on my own while sharing life with others.
prayer2: Lord, thank You for being my strength. Help me to grow in confidence and to share life with others. Amen.
